newsitem.title: CONGO: Heavy shelling tears at Congo ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Heavy shelling tears at Congo ceasefire.

text.p: Artillery fire boomed across the Congolese capital Brazzaville on Monday, shattering a fragile ceasefire as the world tried to cobble together a multi-national force to restore peace to the city.

The shelling and gunfire, the worst breach since the truce took effect on June 17, threatened to undermine efforts by the local mediator, city mayor Bernard Kolelas, to prevent a return to all-out hostilities in the former French colony.

The United Nations is trying to put together a mainly African intervention force for Brazzaville, but insists that the truce must first be rigidly observed. They also demand proof that both sides are committed to finding a political solution.
"There is little new, there has been no progress politically," said Laurent Viguier, number two at the French embassy in Brazzaville, the only Western embassy still open.
Francophone West African nations, holding an economic summit in Togo on Monday, were expected to back the idea of an international buffer force and to offer to take part in it.

The truce, negotiated last week as French troops left the city after evacuating foreign nationals, has stopped political and ethnic clashes that began on June 5. Initially for 72 hours, it was extended to midnight on Thursday.

The clashes have killed hundreds of people, although medical workers have not yet been able to compile an official toll. The capital of the oil-producing Central African nation is carved up into rival strongholds.

No day has gone by without some firing, blamed by mediators on rogue elements in the two rival forces, supporters of President Pascal Lissouba or of his predecessor, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The two men and Kolelas, whose supporters have stayed out of the fighting, were the main contenders in presidential elections that had been due on July 27 but have been postponed indefinitely.
The clashes began after government troops surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home on June 5 as part of efforts to crack down on private militia and unauthorised firearms in the run-up to the election.

A June 16 attempt by Gabon's president Omar Bongo and other African leaders in his capital Libreville to rally the two sides around a peace deal collapsed with mediators highlighting a lack of common ground, particularly on organisation of elections.

Both Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso publicly support the planned intervention force that the United Nations says will need an initial 1,600-1,800 troops to secure the airport and divide the warring parties.
A similar force in Bangui, capital of neighbouring Central African Republic, was caught up in fresh clashes involving disaffected soldiers at the weekend. The clashes killed at least 30 people.

France, which has a defence pact with the Bangui government, refused calls from Lissouba and U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun to leave troops in Brazzaville to act as a buffer force. Its forces pulled out last week after evacuating almost 6,000 French and other foreign nationals.
Two shells from Monday's exchanges landed in the southern Bacongo suburb, a Kolelas stronghold.
Kolelas's militia was at the heart of similar political and ethnic clashes in 1993 after a disputed parliamentary election. Those clashes killed at least 2,000 people.
